controls.label: Color + brightness
controls.qualification: The star's color, darker where K2 saw it dimmer (contrast drawn stronger) · June to August 2014, mapped in this project
controls.notes: K2-18 in its own color, darker where its light in K2's images of June to August 2014 says it was darker. As the star turned once in 36.6 days its light rose and fell by 1.2%. The contrast is drawn far stronger than it is, so the eye can see it: the darkest part gives 3.5% less light than the brightest, and is drawn as a much darker tone of the star's own hue; the Brightness map's scale has the measured values. The longitudes of the darker and brighter parts are measured. Their latitudes and shapes are not: they are the smoothest that reproduce the light. No change of color is drawn, because none is measured. Spots come and go within weeks or months: this is the star then. The darkening toward the edge is the Color dataset's limb law, drawn 1.5 times as strong.

controls.label: Brightness map
controls.qualification: Mapped in this project · K2 mission light curve, campaign 1
controls.notes: Where the star's surface was darker and brighter in K2 campaign 1, worked out in this project from how its light rose and fell by 1.2% as it turned once in 36.6 days. The light curve is the mission's own; Reinhold & Hekker (2020, A&A 635, A43) found the star's rotation in it, and starry finds the map that reproduces it at their period. The longitudes of the dark and bright regions are fixed by the data; their latitudes are not. No tilt of this star's axis is known: the map is made at 60°, the middle tilt of axes that point at random.
controls.legendNote: Darker: dimmer than the star's mean surface; white: brighter.

controls.label: Color
controls.qualification: Color from a measured spectrum of the star (LAMOST). The disc is unresolved; its darker edge follows a model limb-darkening law, not a measurement.
controls.notes: The color of K2-18's LAMOST spectrum. The LAMOST survey telescope observed it on 21 March 2014, with a relative flux calibration and a fibre warning in the file. No resolved image of the surface is cast here.

controls.label: Habitable zone
controls.notes: The star with its habitable zone drawn as a green band in the plane of its planet' orbit. The band is a calculation, not an observation: the distances at which a planet of Earth's mass with a carbon dioxide, water and nitrogen atmosphere could keep liquid water on its surface, by the model of Kopparapu et al. (2013, 2014), as the Habitable Zone Gallery (Kane & Gelino 2012) calculates them from the star's temperature and luminosity. The darker band is the conservative zone, 0.153 to 0.297 au, between the runaway greenhouse and maximum greenhouse limits; the lighter strips extend it to the optimistic zone, 0.120 to 0.313 au, between the recent Venus and early Mars limits. Planet b (0.159 au) lies in the conservative zone. A planet in the zone is not known to be habitable.
